OCCUPATIONAL LICENSING ELIGIBILITY DESPITE CRIMINAL HISTORY — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet states, using the statutes' own text, the framework California Business and Professions Code §§ 480 through 484 and § 7.5 impose on every state licensing board named in that code when the board considers denying an occupational or professional license to Jordan T. Reyes based on the applicant's criminal history, in connection with Jordan T. Reyes's pursuit of licensure as a cosmetology before the Board of Barbering and Cosmetology. It states facts about what the statutes require, permit, and prohibit. It does not predict how Board of Barbering and Cosmetology will apply these standards to Jordan T. Reyes's particular record, and it does not instruct Acme, Inc. or Jordan T. Reyes on what to do about any specific application, disclosure, or denial.

THE TWO GROUNDS ON WHICH A BOARD MAY DENY A LICENSE FOR CRIMINAL HISTORY
Business and Professions Code § 480(a) states that, notwithstanding any other provision of the code, a board may deny a license regulated by the code on the grounds that the applicant has been convicted of a crime or has been subject to formal discipline only if one of two conditions is met. The first, stated in paragraph (a)(1), is that the applicant has been convicted of a crime, within the preceding seven years from the date of application, that is substantially related to the qualifications, functions, or duties of the business or profession for which the application is made — regardless of whether the applicant was incarcerated for that crime — or has been convicted of such a substantially related crime and is presently incarcerated for it or was released from incarceration for it within the preceding seven years.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(a) Notwithstanding any other provision of this code, a board may deny a license regulated by this code on the grounds that the applicant has been convicted of a crime or has been subject to formal discipline only if either of the following conditions are met:(1) The applicant has been convicted of a crime within the preceding seven years from the date of application that is substantially related to the qualifications, functions, or duties of the business or profession for which the application is made, regardless of whether the applicant was incarcerated for that crime, or the applicant has been convicted of a crime that is substantially related to the qualifications, functions, or duties of the business or profession for which the application is made and for which the applicant is presently incarcerated or for which the applicant was released from incarceration within the preceding seven years from the date of application."
  — Business and Professions Code § 480 (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 480(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=480.&lawCode=BPC)
  Known gap: This clause states only the seven-year conviction ground of paragraph (a)(1); it does not state the separate formal-discipline ground of paragraph (a)(2) (a companion clause in this document does), and it does not state the statute's own exceptions removing the seven-year limitation entirely for certain offenses (also a companion clause).

THE SEPARATE FORMAL-DISCIPLINE GROUND, AND ITS OWN CARVE-BACK FOR DISMISSED CONVICTIONS
Business and Professions Code § 480(a)(2) states the second ground on which a board may deny a license: that the applicant has been subjected to formal discipline by a licensing board in or outside California, within the preceding seven years, based on professional misconduct that would have been cause for discipline before the board receiving the present application and that is substantially related to the qualifications, functions, or duties of that business or profession. The statute states its own limit on this ground: prior disciplinary action within the preceding seven years is not a basis for denial if that discipline rested on a conviction that has since been dismissed under Penal Code § 1203.4, 1203.4a, 1203.41, 1203.42, or 1203.425, or a comparable dismissal or expungement. The statute separately states a narrow exception reaching further back than seven years, tied to a comparison against the standard that would apply to a physician and surgeon's sexual misconduct with a patient under Business and Professions Code §§ 726 and 729.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(2) The applicant has been subjected to formal discipline by a licensing board in or outside California within the preceding seven years from the date of application based on professional misconduct that would have been cause for discipline before the board for which the present application is made and that is substantially related to the qualifications, functions, or duties of the business or profession for which the present application is made. However, prior disciplinary action by a licensing board within the preceding seven years shall not be the basis for denial of a license if the basis for that disciplinary action was a conviction that has been dismissed pursuant to Section 1203.4, 1203.4a, 1203.41, 1203.42, or 1203.425 of the Penal Code or a comparable dismissal or expungement. Formal discipline that occurred earlier than seven years preceding the date of application may be grounds for denial of a license only if the formal discipline was for conduct that, if committed in this state by a physician and surgeon licensed pursuant to Chapter 5 (commencing with Section 2000) of Division 2, would have constituted an act of sexual abuse, misconduct, or relations with a patient pursuant to Section 726 or sexual exploitation as defined in subdivision (a) of Section 729."
  — Business and Professions Code § 480 (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 480(a)(2) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=480.&lawCode=BPC)
  Known gap: The 'would have constituted an act of sexual abuse, misconduct, or relations with a patient' comparator is stated by cross-reference to Sections 726 and 729; this clause does not independently verify or reproduce the text of either of those sections, which a board applying this older-than-seven-years exception would need to consult.

WHEN THE SEVEN-YEAR LIMITATION ON THE CONVICTION GROUND DOES NOT APPLY
Business and Professions Code § 480(a)(1) states two situations in which the seven-year limitation on the conviction ground for denial does not apply at all, meaning a conviction of any age may be considered. The first is a conviction of a 'serious felony' as defined in Penal Code § 1192.7, or a crime requiring registration under Penal Code § 290(d)(2) or (3). The second is a conviction of a financial crime currently classified as a felony that is directly and adversely related to the fiduciary duties of the profession, under regulations the particular board has adopted, and only for applicants seeking licensure under specifically named chapters of the code — including State Bar-adjacent fiduciary licensure categories, funeral director or cemetery manager licensure, and Division 4 licensure (real estate).

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "However, the preceding seven-year limitation shall not apply in either of the following situations:(A) The applicant was convicted of a serious felony, as defined in Section 1192.7 of the Penal Code or a crime for which registration is required pursuant to paragraph (2) or (3) of subdivision (d) of Section 290 of the Penal Code.(B) The applicant was convicted of a financial crime currently classified as a felony that is directly and adversely related to the fiduciary qualifications, functions, or duties of the business or profession for which the application is made, pursuant to regulations adopted by the board, and for which the applicant is seeking licensure under any of the following:(i) Chapter 6 (commencing with Section 6500) of Division 3.(ii) Chapter 9 (commencing with Section 7000) of Division 3.(iii) Chapter 11.3 (commencing with Section 7512) of Division 3.(iv) Licensure as a funeral director or cemetery manager under Chapter 12 (commencing with Section 7600) of Division 3.(v) Division 4 (commencing with Section 10000)."
  — Business and Professions Code § 480 (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 480(a)(1)(A)-(B) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=480.&lawCode=BPC)
  Known gap: This clause does not independently verify which occupations fall within each of the five named chapters and divisions listed in subparagraph (B) (i)-(v); a reader would need to consult Chapter 6 commencing with § 6500, Chapter 9 commencing with § 7000, Chapter 11.3 commencing with § 7512, Chapter 12 commencing with § 7600, and Division 4 commencing with § 10000 directly to identify the specific licensed occupations the financial-crime exception reaches.

THE THREE STATUTORY CRITERIA FOR 'SUBSTANTIALLY RELATED'
Business and Professions Code § 481 requires every board under the code to develop criteria to determine whether a crime is substantially related to the qualifications, functions, or duties of the business or profession it regulates — the standard that § 480 uses without independently defining. Subdivision (b) states that these board-level criteria must include, at minimum, three factors: the nature and gravity of the offense; the number of years elapsed since the date of the offense; and the nature and duties of the profession in which the applicant seeks licensure or in which the licensee is licensed. Subdivision (d), not reproduced here, separately requires each board to post a summary of its criteria on its own website.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(b) Criteria for determining whether a crime is substantially related to the qualifications, functions, or duties of the business or profession a board regulates shall include all of the following:(1) The nature and gravity of the offense.(2) The number of years elapsed since the date of the offense.(3) The nature and duties of the profession in which the applicant seeks licensure or in which the licensee is licensed."
  — Business and Professions Code § 481 (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 481(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=481.&lawCode=BPC)
  Known gap: Section 481 requires each board to develop its own criteria consistent with these three minimum statutory factors; this clause does not state, and cannot state generically across all boards, the specific substantially-related criteria any particular licensing board has actually adopted and posted under subdivision (d) — those must be located on that board's own website.

CERTIFICATE OF REHABILITATION, PARDON, OR BOARD SHOWING OF REHABILITATION BARS DENIAL
Business and Professions Code § 480(b) states that a person shall not be denied a license on the basis of a conviction, or the acts underlying it, if the person has obtained a certificate of rehabilitation under Penal Code §§ 4852.01 et seq., has been granted clemency or a pardon by a state or federal executive, or has made a showing of rehabilitation under § 482. Section 482, in turn, requires every board to develop criteria to evaluate rehabilitation for this purpose, and states that a board must consider a person to have made a showing of rehabilitation if either the person completed the criminal sentence at issue without a parole or probation violation, or the board — applying its own rehabilitation criteria — finds the applicant rehabilitated.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(b) Notwithstanding any other provision of this code, a person shall not be denied a license on the basis that the person has been convicted of a crime, or on the basis of acts underlying a conviction for a crime, if that person has obtained a certificate of rehabilitation under Chapter 3.5 (commencing with Section 4852.01) of Title 6 of Part 3 of the Penal Code, has been granted clemency or a pardon by a state or federal executive, or has made a showing of rehabilitation pursuant to Section 482."
  — Business and Professions Code § 480 (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 480(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=480.&lawCode=BPC)
  "(a) Each board under this code shall develop criteria to evaluate the rehabilitation of a person when doing either of the following:(1) Considering the denial of a license by the board under Section 480.(2) Considering suspension or revocation of a license under Section 490.(b) Each board shall consider whether an applicant or licensee has made a showing of rehabilitation if either of the following are met:(1) The applicant or licensee has completed the criminal sentence at issue without a violation of parole or probation.(2) The board, applying its criteria for rehabilitation, finds that the applicant is rehabilitated."
  — Business and Professions Code § 482 (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 482(a)-(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=482.&lawCode=BPC)
  Known gap: This clause does not state the substantive rehabilitation criteria any particular board has adopted under § 482(a), only the statute's floor requirement that completing a sentence without a parole or probation violation must itself count as a showing of rehabilitation; a board's own published criteria may recognize additional or different pathways.

A DISMISSED OR EXPUNGED CONVICTION CANNOT BE A BASIS FOR DENIAL
Business and Professions Code § 480(c) states that a person shall not be denied a license on the basis of any conviction, or the acts underlying it, that has been dismissed under Penal Code § 1203.4, 1203.4a, 1203.41, 1203.42, or 1203.425, or a comparable dismissal or expungement. The statute places a documentation burden on the applicant: an applicant with a conviction dismissed under §§ 1203.4, 1203.4a, 1203.41, or 1203.42 must provide proof of the dismissal if it is not already reflected on the criminal history report the Department of Justice furnishes to the board.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(c) Notwithstanding any other provision of this code, a person shall not be denied a license on the basis of any conviction, or on the basis of the acts underlying the conviction, that has been dismissed pursuant to Section 1203.4, 1203.4a, 1203.41, 1203.42, or 1203.425 of the Penal Code, or a comparable dismissal or expungement. An applicant who has a conviction that has been dismissed pursuant to Section 1203.4, 1203.4a, 1203.41, or 1203.42 of the Penal Code shall provide proof of the dismissal if it is not reflected on the report furnished by the Department of Justice."
  — Business and Professions Code § 480 (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 480(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=480.&lawCode=BPC)
  Known gap: The statute's list of qualifying dismissal mechanisms in the first sentence includes § 1203.425, but the applicant's own proof-of-dismissal obligation in the second sentence is stated only for §§ 1203.4, 1203.4a, 1203.41, and 1203.42 — the statute's own text does not extend that specific proof obligation to a § 1203.425 dismissal or to an unnamed 'comparable dismissal or expungement,' and this clause does not resolve that asymmetry.

ARRESTS WITHOUT CONVICTION, INFRACTIONS, CITATIONS, AND JUVENILE ADJUDICATIONS CANNOT BE A BASIS FOR DENIAL
Business and Professions Code § 480(d) states that a board shall not deny a license on the basis of an arrest that resulted in a disposition other than a conviction, including an arrest that resulted in an infraction, a citation, or a juvenile adjudication.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(d) Notwithstanding any other provision of this code, a board shall not deny a license on the basis of an arrest that resulted in a disposition other than a conviction, including an arrest that resulted in an infraction, citation, or a juvenile adjudication."
  — Business and Professions Code § 480 (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 480(d) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=480.&lawCode=BPC)
  Known gap: This subdivision restricts what a board may use as a basis for denying a license; it does not, by its own text, restrict what a board may ask an applicant on a license application — that separate disclosure question is governed by § 480(f), stated in a companion clause of this document.

MOST BOARDS MAY NOT REQUIRE DISCLOSURE OF CRIMINAL HISTORY ON THE APPLICATION AT ALL
Business and Professions Code § 480(f) states the procedures a board must follow in requesting or acting on an applicant's criminal history information. Paragraph (f)(1) names a specific, limited list of code chapters and divisions whose boards may require applicants to disclose criminal conviction history on a license application. Paragraph (f)(2) states the default rule for every other board: except as provided in paragraph (1), a board shall not require an applicant to disclose any information or documentation regarding the applicant's criminal history at all — though a board may request mitigating information voluntarily, provided the applicant is told the disclosure is voluntary and that declining to disclose will not itself count against the application.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(f) A board shall follow the following procedures in requesting or acting on an applicant’s criminal history information:(1) A board issuing a license pursuant to Chapter 3 (commencing with Section 5500), Chapter 3.5 (commencing with Section 5615), Chapter 10 (commencing with Section 7301), Chapter 20 (commencing with Section 9800), or Chapter 20.3 (commencing with Section 9880), of Division 3, or Chapter 3 (commencing with Section 19000) or Chapter 3.1 (commencing with Section 19225) of Division 8 may require applicants for licensure under those chapters to disclose criminal conviction history on an application for licensure.(2) Except as provided in paragraph (1), a board shall not require an applicant for licensure to disclose any information or documentation regarding the applicant’s criminal history. However, a board may request mitigating information from an applicant regarding the applicant’s criminal history for purposes of determining substantial relation or demonstrating evidence of rehabilitation, provided that the applicant is informed that disclosure is voluntary and that the applicant’s decision not to disclose any information shall not be a factor in a board’s decision to grant or deny an application for licensure."
  — Business and Professions Code § 480 (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 480(f)(1)-(2) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=480.&lawCode=BPC)
  Known gap: This clause does not independently verify which occupations the seven named chapters and divisions in paragraph (f)(1) cover (Chapter 3 commencing with § 5500, Chapter 3.5 commencing with § 5615, Chapter 10 commencing with § 7301, Chapter 20 commencing with § 9800, and Chapter 20.3 commencing with § 9880 of Division 3, and Chapter 3 commencing with § 19000 and Chapter 3.1 commencing with § 19225 of Division 8); whether a given applicant's board falls inside or outside that list determines which of the two very different disclosure rules applies, and that must be checked against the named chapters directly.

REQUIRED WRITTEN NOTICE WHEN A BOARD DENIES A LICENSE FOR CONVICTION HISTORY
Business and Professions Code § 480(f)(3) states that if a board decides to deny a license application based solely or in part on the applicant's conviction history, the board shall notify the applicant in writing of four things: the denial or disqualification of licensure; any existing board procedure to challenge the decision or request reconsideration; that the applicant has the right to appeal the board's decision; and the process for the applicant to request a copy of their complete conviction history and question its accuracy or completeness under Penal Code §§ 11122 through 11127.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(3) If a board decides to deny an application for licensure based solely or in part on the applicant’s conviction history, the board shall notify the applicant in writing of all of the following:(A) The denial or disqualification of licensure.(B) Any existing procedure the board has for the applicant to challenge the decision or to request reconsideration.(C) That the applicant has the right to appeal the board’s decision.(D) The processes for the applicant to request a copy of the applicant’s complete conviction history and question the accuracy or completeness of the record pursuant to Sections 11122 to 11127 of the Penal Code."
  — Business and Professions Code § 480 (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 480(f)(3) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=480.&lawCode=BPC)
  Known gap: This clause states only the four items the written notice must contain; it does not state a deadline by which the board must send that notice, nor the substantive procedures (challenge, reconsideration, or appeal) any particular board has adopted to implement subparagraph (B) and (C) — those procedures vary by board and are outside this clause's scope.

A SINGLE STATUTORY DEFINITION OF 'CONVICTION' CONTROLS, WITH A NAMED EXCEPTION
Business and Professions Code § 7.5(a) defines 'conviction,' for purposes of the code, as a judgment following a plea or verdict of guilty, a plea of nolo contendere, or a finding of guilt. The statute states that an action a board is permitted to take following a conviction may be taken once the time for appeal has elapsed, once the conviction is affirmed on appeal, or once an order granting probation suspends imposition of sentence — but that a board may not deny a license to an applicant otherwise qualified under § 480(b) or (c) (the rehabilitation and dismissed-conviction protections stated in companion clauses of this document). Section 7.5(c) states that, except as provided in subdivision (b), this definition controls over and supersedes the definition of 'conviction' contained within individual practice acts elsewhere in the code. Subdivision (b)(1) states one named exception: nothing in § 7.5 applies to licensure of persons under Chapter 4 (commencing with § 6000) of Division 3 — the State Bar Act governing attorney licensure.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(a) A conviction within the meaning of this code means a judgment following a plea or verdict of guilty or a plea of nolo contendere or finding of guilt. Any action which a board is permitted to take following the establishment of a conviction may be taken when the time for appeal has elapsed, or the judgment of conviction has been affirmed on appeal or when an order granting probation is made suspending the imposition of sentence. However, a board may not deny a license to an applicant who is otherwise qualified pursuant to subdivision (b) or (c) of Section 480."
  — Business and Professions Code § 7.5 (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7.5(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=7.5.&lawCode=BPC)
  "(b) (1) Nothing in this section shall apply to the licensure of persons pursuant to Chapter 4 (commencing with Section 6000) of Division 3."
  — Business and Professions Code § 7.5 (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7.5(b)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=7.5.&lawCode=BPC)
  "(c) Except as provided in subdivision (b), this section controls over and supersedes the definition of conviction contained within individual practice acts under this code."
  — Business and Professions Code § 7.5 (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7.5(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=7.5.&lawCode=BPC)
  Known gap: This clause quotes subdivision (b)(1)'s State Bar exception and subdivision (c)'s general controls-and-supersedes rule as two separate citations because the intervening text of subdivision (b)(2), naming the State Athletic Commission, the Bureau for Private Postsecondary Education, and the California Horse Racing Board as further exceptions, is not reproduced verbatim here; a reader needing the complete list of entities subdivision (b) exempts should consult the statute's full text directly.

NO BOARD MAY REQUIRE THIRD-PARTY ATTESTATIONS OF GOOD MORAL CHARACTER
Business and Professions Code § 484 states that no person applying for licensure under the code shall be required to submit to any licensing board any attestation by other persons to their good moral character.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "No person applying for licensure under this code shall be required to submit to any licensing board any attestation by other persons to his good moral character."
  — Business and Professions Code § 484 (California Legislative Information text), Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 484 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=484.&lawCode=BPC)
  Known gap: This section, last amended in 1974, bars a board from requiring third-party character attestations as a submission requirement; its brief text does not address, and this clause does not resolve, whether a board may still ask the applicant to self-attest to their own good moral character, or may independently investigate character through other statutorily authorized channels such as the criminal-history procedures stated in § 480(f).

CERTIFICATION
This information sheet was prepared for Acme, Inc. regarding Jordan T. Reyes's pursuit of licensure as a cosmetology before the Board of Barbering and Cosmetology in connection with the position of Licensed Cosmetologist, and reflects the statutory text current as of the date below. It states facts about Business and Professions Code §§ 480-484 and § 7.5; it is not a determination of Jordan T. Reyes's eligibility for any specific license and does not substitute for consulting Board of Barbering and Cosmetology directly.

Prepared/reviewed by: ______________________
Date: September 6, 2026

expectedJSON.body: Business and Professions Code § 480(b) states that a person shall not be denied a license on the basis of a conviction, or the acts underlying it, if the person has obtained a certificate of rehabilitation under Penal Code §§ 4852.01 et seq., has been granted clemency or a pardon by a state or federal executive, or has made a showing of rehabilitation under § 482. Section 482, in turn, requires every board to develop criteria to evaluate rehabilitation for this purpose, and states that a board must consider a person to have made a showing of rehabilitation if either the person completed the criminal sentence at issue without a parole or probation violation, or the board — applying its own rehabilitation criteria — finds the applicant rehabilitated.

citations.case: Business and Professions Code § 480 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (b) Notwithstanding any other provision of this code, a person shall not be denied a license on the basis that the person has been convicted of a crime, or on the basis of acts underlying a conviction for a crime, if that person has obtained a certificate of rehabilitation under Chapter 3.5 (commencing with Section 4852.01) of Title 6 of Part 3 of the Penal Code, has been granted clemency or a pardon by a state or federal executive, or has made a showing of rehabilitation pursuant to Section 482.

citations.case: Business and Professions Code § 482 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (a) Each board under this code shall develop criteria to evaluate the rehabilitation of a person when doing either of the following:(1) Considering the denial of a license by the board under Section 480.(2) Considering suspension or revocation of a license under Section 490.(b) Each board shall consider whether an applicant or licensee has made a showing of rehabilitation if either of the following are met:(1) The applicant or licensee has completed the criminal sentence at issue without a violation of parole or probation.(2) The board, applying its criteria for rehabilitation, finds that the applicant is rehabilitated.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause does not state the substantive rehabilitation criteria any particular board has adopted under § 482(a), only the statute's floor requirement that completing a sentence without a parole or probation violation must itself count as a showing of rehabilitation; a board's own published criteria may recognize additional or different pathways.

expectedJSON.body: Business and Professions Code § 480(f) states the procedures a board must follow in requesting or acting on an applicant's criminal history information. Paragraph (f)(1) names a specific, limited list of code chapters and divisions whose boards may require applicants to disclose criminal conviction history on a license application. Paragraph (f)(2) states the default rule for every other board: except as provided in paragraph (1), a board shall not require an applicant to disclose any information or documentation regarding the applicant's criminal history at all — though a board may request mitigating information voluntarily, provided the applicant is told the disclosure is voluntary and that declining to disclose will not itself count against the application.

citations.case: Business and Professions Code § 480 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (f) A board shall follow the following procedures in requesting or acting on an applicant’s criminal history information:(1) A board issuing a license pursuant to Chapter 3 (commencing with Section 5500), Chapter 3.5 (commencing with Section 5615), Chapter 10 (commencing with Section 7301), Chapter 20 (commencing with Section 9800), or Chapter 20.3 (commencing with Section 9880), of Division 3, or Chapter 3 (commencing with Section 19000) or Chapter 3.1 (commencing with Section 19225) of Division 8 may require applicants for licensure under those chapters to disclose criminal conviction history on an application for licensure.(2) Except as provided in paragraph (1), a board shall not require an applicant for licensure to disclose any information or documentation regarding the applicant’s criminal history. However, a board may request mitigating information from an applicant regarding the applicant’s criminal history for purposes of determining substantial relation or demonstrating evidence of rehabilitation, provided that the applicant is informed that disclosure is voluntary and that the applicant’s decision not to disclose any information shall not be a factor in a board’s decision to grant or deny an application for licensure.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause does not independently verify which occupations the seven named chapters and divisions in paragraph (f)(1) cover (Chapter 3 commencing with § 5500, Chapter 3.5 commencing with § 5615, Chapter 10 commencing with § 7301, Chapter 20 commencing with § 9800, and Chapter 20.3 commencing with § 9880 of Division 3, and Chapter 3 commencing with § 19000 and Chapter 3.1 commencing with § 19225 of Division 8); whether a given applicant's board falls inside or outside that list determines which of the two very different disclosure rules applies, and that must be checked against the named chapters directly.

citations.quote: (3) If a board decides to deny an application for licensure based solely or in part on the applicant’s conviction history, the board shall notify the applicant in writing of all of the following:(A) The denial or disqualification of licensure.(B) Any existing procedure the board has for the applicant to challenge the decision or to request reconsideration.(C) That the applicant has the right to appeal the board’s decision.(D) The processes for the applicant to request a copy of the applicant’s complete conviction history and question the accuracy or completeness of the record pursuant to Sections 11122 to 11127 of the Penal Code.

expectedJSON.body: Business and Professions Code § 7.5(a) defines 'conviction,' for purposes of the code, as a judgment following a plea or verdict of guilty, a plea of nolo contendere, or a finding of guilt. The statute states that an action a board is permitted to take following a conviction may be taken once the time for appeal has elapsed, once the conviction is affirmed on appeal, or once an order granting probation suspends imposition of sentence — but that a board may not deny a license to an applicant otherwise qualified under § 480(b) or (c) (the rehabilitation and dismissed-conviction protections stated in companion clauses of this document). Section 7.5(c) states that, except as provided in subdivision (b), this definition controls over and supersedes the definition of 'conviction' contained within individual practice acts elsewhere in the code. Subdivision (b)(1) states one named exception: nothing in § 7.5 applies to licensure of persons under Chapter 4 (commencing with § 6000) of Division 3 — the State Bar Act governing attorney licensure.

citations.case: Business and Professions Code § 7.5 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (a) A conviction within the meaning of this code means a judgment following a plea or verdict of guilty or a plea of nolo contendere or finding of guilt. Any action which a board is permitted to take following the establishment of a conviction may be taken when the time for appeal has elapsed, or the judgment of conviction has been affirmed on appeal or when an order granting probation is made suspending the imposition of sentence. However, a board may not deny a license to an applicant who is otherwise qualified pursuant to subdivision (b) or (c) of Section 480.

citations.case: Business and Professions Code § 7.5 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (b) (1) Nothing in this section shall apply to the licensure of persons pursuant to Chapter 4 (commencing with Section 6000) of Division 3.
